title: 20 Rules to Lead By
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles, a school curriculum and department leader, offers twenty compact rules for leading a team through curriculum improvement. His themes are iteration over perfection, repeated communication, counting what you value and reading averages critically, and protecting limited time by fixing a rotating review cycle of six priorities. He argues that curriculum development changes teachers faster than slow, one-teacher-at-a-time CPD, and he proposes meeting shortcuts such as one-page rationales and anonymous percentage-agreement voting. Other rules push leaders to judge teaching by what students do rather than by subjective lesson observation, to share model answers, to test long-term memory and to standardise the curriculum while giving each teacher one unit a year to experiment with. The move is to replace opinion and initiative overload with measurement, shared resources and team accountability.
points: Plan for impact rather than perfection: launch quickly, measure early and keep iterating, which also lets teachers contribute improvements without it reading as leader failure.
Repeat every message about six times and put numbers on the things you value so you can tell whether they are working.
Decide in meetings with a one-page rationale and percentage-agreement votes, keeping discussion for the cases where someone disagrees.
Judge teaching by student work and assessment progress because lesson-observation ratings agree only about half the time.
Standardise the curriculum and resources across the team, but give each teacher one unit a year to experiment with.
quotes: Nothing works. Iterate. Expect everything to have teething problems. It doesn’t matter how thoroughly or perfectly you plan, it’s still going to go wrong. Don’t plan for perfect, plan for impact.
Your communication is rubbish. Saying it doesn’t make it so. You need to revisit each message 6 times before it can be heard through the noise.
CPD is slow. CPD changes only one willing teacher at a time. 20% are willing. 20% are opposed. 60% are swing voters.
Everyone then writes a percentage agreement on a postage note. If everyone scores 75% or more, it is carried. No discussion necessary.
The curriculum isn’t what you’ve planned, it’s what students do. Look at books as a team, and ask which students and classes know more, and can do more.
Teaching is subjective. When we watch teachers, we instinctively rate them. Yet research shows we only agree 50% of the time.

Standardise the curriculum. If everyone teaches the same content, from the same resources, booklets and lesson plans; if teachers write this curriculum together … every teacher will teach well-designed lessons.
